editorial.summary: DVDASA's first call-in experiment is hosted by David Choe with Alex Tarrant, Critter, Valentin, and Bobby Namba; Asa Akira is absent for work. A Burner app number, an iPhone on speakerphone, no screening, and no reliable speaker separation make provenance the episode's central problem. Callers give names, locations, military assignments, marriages, workplaces, pregnancies, sexual histories, and career details, but none is independently authenticated and none belongs in searchable people metadata. The opening caller is forced through racial stereotypes to prove he is Black. “Baby Cakes” receives a coercive answer to a sexual question; the editorial layer preserves it but explicitly refuses it as advice. A Navy caller describes hydraulics training and the USS Ohio, a New Orleans couple discusses a fifteen-year relationship, a Daly City caller is berated for weak answers, and a home-health nurse is pushed to disclose his wife's body and their sex life. A Philadelphia eighteen-year-old calls wheat-pasting street art; David attacks the terminology and work schedule. The record preserves both practices rather than silently adopting one speaker's gatekeeping. A Chicago caller discusses an interracial marriage and a coming child. Comic recommendations repair Preacher, Scalped, Jason Aaron, R. M. Guéra, and Mark Millar; a provisional San Diego Comic-Con appearance leads to In the Mix in Poway and a tribute to Asa's production labor. An Ohio Kia salesperson with a Kent State glass-art degree is pushed to pinpoint when his “soul died”; David tells him to abandon his family, destroy dealership property, enter an institution, and make art. That is improvised provocation, not career, mental-health, or family guidance. The last third moves away from callers into bullying and retaliation. A Washington-area airport line prompts threats toward fourteen-year-olds. David recalls racial abuse near Andre's Italian Restaurant and the Original Farmers Market; Bobby remembers a hockey concussion; David describes striking children while skating; Critter gives a compressed account of fighting five adults. David then recounts diversion work, his grandmother's death, killing pigeons, conflict with a pseudonymous younger classmate, following her home, recording family movements and license plates, and using intimidation. A later sexual-assault and pregnancy claim about that private person is unverified, presented with laughter, and must never become biography or a searchable allegation. Racial misidentification at an airport and in Switzerland culminates in the Ai Weiwei comparison and a search for better responses. One empty cleaner drop is safe; forty-six contextual decisions improve the text; 2,644 identity windows remain intact and named dialogue is withheld.
